description: Job Description Introduction Established in 1951, IOM is a Related Organization of the United Nations and the leading UN agency in the field of migration. Working closely with governmental, intergovernmental and non-governmental partners, IOM promotes humane and orderly migration for the benefit of all. It saves lives and protects people on the move, drives solutions to displacement, and facilitates pathways for regular migration, while providing services and advice to governments and migrants. IOM is committed to fostering a respectful, inclusive and supportive workplace where all employees can thrive professionally and feel valued. By creating such an environment, IOM aims to better harness the full potential of migration and strengthen its support to people on the move. IOM invites candidates from diverse backgrounds to apply and provides reasonable accommodation throughout the recruitment process when required. Learn more about IOM’s workplace culture at IOM workplace culture | International Organization for Migration Project Context and Scope Established in 1951, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is the leading intergovernmental organization in the field of migration and works closely with governmental, intergovernmental and non-governmental partners. IOM is committed to promoting humane and orderly migration for the benefit of all by providing services and advice to governments and migrants. As a member of the United Nations system, IOM supports governments globally to strengthen migration management systems, enhance border governance, improve service delivery and reinforce institutional capacities in line with international standards. In July 2026, IOM Ethiopia began implementation of the Regional Counter-Smuggling Programme (RCSP) in the East and Horn of Africa, funded by the United Kingdom Home Office. The Programme aims to strengthen airport border management capacities and regional cooperation to address document fraud, migrant smuggling and related forms of transnational organized crime in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Somalia. The programme promotes evidence-based policy and institutional approaches, regional cooperation, gender equality and protection-sensitive responses. In Ethiopia, the RCSP supports the Government in strengthening aviation border management capacities, improving the detection of fraudulent travel documents and enhancing the ability of frontline institutions to identify and respond to trafficking in persons, migrant smuggling and related forms of transnational organized crime. Integrating gender equality, disability inclusion, social inclusion and protection considerations into border management can further support effective operations and contribute to services that respond appropriately to the different needs and circumstances of travellers and migrants, including persons in vulnerable situations. According to the Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance (DCAF) publication Tool 6: Border Management and Gender (2020), increasing women’s representation within border management and law enforcement institutions can generate important operational and institutional benefits. Gender-diverse institutions may be better positioned to understand and respond to the different needs, experiences and vulnerabilities of women, men, girls and boys, including victims of trafficking in persons, migrant smuggling and other forms of exploitation. Female border and law enforcement officers can also play an important role in conducting gender-sensitive interviews and lawful searches of female travellers, particularly where cultural, religious or social norms may affect interactions between women and male officers. Representative and inclusive institutions can contribute to public trust and may encourage women and other persons in vulnerable situations to seek assistance, report incidents and share information relevant to the prevention and detection of trafficking in persons, migrant smuggling and related crime. The overall objective of this consultancy is to assesses how relevant national institutional priorities concerning gender equality are reflected in the legal, policy, human resource and operational arrangements of ICS. The assessment will identify and document existing measures that support women’s recruitment, retention, professional development, career progression and leadership; examine practical experiences and challenges; and identify opportunities for further strengthening. It will use available institutional information and consultations with relevant personnel. Where relevant and feasible, consultations and operational observations may include experiences at Bole International Airport and Dire Dawa International Airport, which are among the airports targeted by the RCSP in Ethiopia. The consultant will develop practical, evidence-based recommendations and possible outreach or institutional measures to support women’s participation and advancement within ICS. Responsib
